items.stem: Scenario: A retailer wants to answer shoppers' questions about delivery dates, using a feed that its own code already queries. Each question needs one lookup and one reply, never more. Which rung fits?

options.a: A team of agents, since several shoppers ask at the same moment of the day
options.b: An augmented call, since one outside fact and a single step suffice
options.c: An agent that chooses its own tools, since flexibility is worth buying
options.d: A workflow of five calls, since more calls give a more accurate reply

items.explanation: One outside fact and one step is the augmented call. A workflow suits steps that differ in kind, and an agent or a team is bought only by a stated requirement.

items.stem: Scenario: A claims sponsor says the project exists so that processing a finished claim takes less money than last year. Which value pillar is that, and what is the yardstick?

options.a: Efficiency, measured by handling time per claim against last quarter
options.b: Productivity, measured by hours saved per person each working week
options.c: Transformation, measured by the share of customers served in a new way
options.d: Cost, per completed task versus the human baseline

items.explanation: The cost pillar claims that work costs less in total, and it counts tokens, review time and rework against the human baseline, not model price alone.

items.stem: Scenario: A small trial of a drafting assistant with ten users succeeded. Before it goes to three thousand staff, the architect must say what the plan needs.

options.a: Name each friendly condition that fails at scale, with a test and a trigger
options.b: Order three thousand licences and train the staff during the first month of the rollout
options.c: Replace the model with a larger one before the wider launch begins
options.d: Repeat the trial with more volunteers until the results stop changing

items.explanation: Scale changes the surroundings, so the plan names the assumptions that held only in friendly conditions, each with a test and a trigger that stops the roll-out.

items.stem: Scenario: A proposal shows an input stage, a processing stage and an output stage that checks every result, but nothing that turns users' corrections into changes. Which stage is missing, and how serious is it in the course's review?

options.a: Output, a medium finding that asks for a revision of the design
options.b: Feedback, a low finding that is only recorded in the report for later
options.c: Feedback, a high finding that rejects the design until it is added
options.d: Input, a high finding that rejects the design until it is added

items.explanation: The four stages are input, processing, output and feedback. A missing feedback stage is a high finding, and a design with any high finding is rejected.

items.stem: Scenario: Three subagents each research a different supplier, but two of them return the same findings and one supplier is missed. What was most likely weak in the lead's brief to them?

options.a: The model size of the subagents, which was too small for the sources
options.b: The retry limit, which was too low for the search tool they used
options.c: The checkpoint store, which did not keep the first results they found
options.d: The task description, which lacked an objective and boundaries

items.explanation: A vague task description makes subagents duplicate work or leave gaps. A brief states the objective, the output format, the tools and the boundaries.

items.stem: Scenario: A research task has independent parts, needs more reading than one context holds, and is worth about thirty chats. A reviewer asks whether a team of agents pays. What is the answer?

options.a: No, since a team always costs more than the work is worth
options.b: No, since only agents that share a context can reach that value in practice
options.c: Yes, since independence, volume and value all clear the bar of fifteen
options.d: Yes, but only after a single agent has failed on the task twice

items.explanation: A team needs independent parts, a volume above one context and a value that pays the multiple of about 15 chats. All three hold here.

items.stem: Scenario: A payment tool times out after the transfer was made, and the agent's retry returns the stored receipt without moving money again. What made the second call safe?

options.a: A key that names the intended action, saved in one step with the effect
options.b: A longer timeout on the call, so that the first answer always arrives in time
options.c: A prompt rule telling the agent not to pay the same order twice
options.d: A fresh key for each retry, so that the tool never mixes attempts up

items.explanation: An idempotency key names the intention and is recorded together with the effect, so a repeat returns the first result instead of acting again.

items.stem: Scenario: A plan has tasks a, b, c and d, where d needs c. Task c fails for good while a and b finish. What does the final report show?

options.a: Everything failed, since one broken part makes the rest untrustworthy
options.b: a and b done, c broken with a cause, d skipped because of c
options.c: a, b and d done, with d computed from a guess at c's result
options.d: a and b done, with c and d left out of the report

items.explanation: A failure stays in its branch: only the task that needs the failed one is skipped, with a reason that names it, and the report lists done, failed and skipped apart.

items.stem: Scenario: A batch of ten jobs stops on an unexpected error in the last one, after nine have finished. What is the right handling?

options.a: Catch the error and carry on, reporting the batch as complete
options.b: Fix the cause, then resume from the results already stored
options.c: Start the batch again so that every result is made fresh
options.d: Discard the stored results, since a stop makes them untrustworthy

items.explanation: A crash is not caught: the process stops, the cause is fixed and the run resumes, because finished results were written as work was done.

items.stem: Scenario: A support prompt puts today's date and the customer's name in its first line, followed by 12,000 tokens of policy. The cache never hits. What is the cause?

options.a: The policy is too long to be cached on any current model
options.b: The date is counted as a dynamic module, which cannot be cached at all
options.c: A changing value sits in front of the stable text, so no prefix matches
options.d: The cache lifetime is shorter than the gap between two customers

items.explanation: Two requests share a cache entry only when everything up to the breakpoint is identical, so a changing value in the prefix breaks every match.

items.stem: Scenario: A team plans to run its biggest offering for a nightly job that tags 200,000 tickets, because quality matters most. Which approach fits the page?

options.a: Choose the cheapest model that reaches the tier and the latency limit
options.b: Keep the largest, since the business cares most about quality
options.c: Pick the smallest model available, whatever its quality turns out to be
options.d: Use the largest for the first month and then drop one size

items.explanation: The rule is the cheapest model among those whose tier is at least the workload's and whose latency is within the limit; price ranks only the models that are already right.

items.stem: Scenario: A prompt puts the rules, three sample cases and the incoming message in one block of plain text, and the model sometimes treats a sample as a rule. Which repair does the prompting guide support?

options.a: Add a stronger sentence saying that the samples are not rules
options.b: Remove the samples, since few-shot cases never help a model
options.c: Move everything into the user turn, in a different order
options.d: Wrap the examples and the changing input in their own tags

items.explanation: Tags separate instructions, context, examples and variable input, which reduces misreading in a prompt that mixes them.

items.stem: Scenario: A customer needs its processing to stay inside the EU. The team deploys on a cloud platform and picks a model. What is the check?

options.a: That the model's name contains the letters eu
options.b: That the inference geography is pinned to global
options.c: That the region string of the setup names a European location
options.d: That the workspace geography is set to a European value

items.explanation: On the cloud platforms the region is part of the deployment, and the check is on the region string. The Claude API has no European pin.

items.stem: Scenario: An architect designs the audit entry written for each call of a claims assistant. Which contents fit the course's design?

options.a: Request id, text size, count of identifiers swapped and a no-prompt flag
options.b: Request id, the full prompt and the reply, kept for the ceiling period
options.c: The reply only, since it is the output the customer received
options.d: The prompt with identifiers masked by asterisks, kept for the floor period

items.explanation: The log proves what happened without becoming a second store of the data: ids, sizes, counts and a flag, never the prompt.

items.stem: Scenario: A company that has zero data retention for its main organisation opens another organisation for a fresh product. What follows?

options.a: It inherits the arrangement, since the company is the same legal entity
options.b: It is covered once the first organisation renews its agreement
options.c: It needs no request, since zero retention is a property of the model
options.d: It needs its own request to Anthropic, since the setting is per account

items.explanation: Zero data retention is an arrangement with Anthropic, enabled per organisation, so each new organisation needs its own.

items.stem: Scenario: A prompt of 7,700 input tokens has 6,000 read from the cache, 200 written and 1,500 uncached. How many tokens count toward the input limit?

options.a: 7,700, since every input token counts toward the limit
options.b: 1,700, the fresh part plus what was stored
options.c: 1,500, since cache writes are billed but not counted
options.d: 6,200, the cached tokens plus the writes

items.explanation: For most models only uncached input and cache writes count toward ITPM; cache reads do not, so caching moves the binding limit.

items.stem: Scenario: Calls from a company's assistant begin to return 529 errors while its own usage is far below every limit it holds. What does that mean, and what should the design do?

options.a: The spend cap was reached, so stop retrying and alert a person at once
options.b: Capacity trouble at the provider, so retry with backoff or use a fallback
options.c: A rate limit was hit, so wait for the time that the response gives
options.d: The key was revoked, so issue a new key and retry the call at once

items.explanation: A 529 means the service is overloaded, which is not the team's limit. A rate-limit 429 gives a wait time, and a spend-cap 429 must not be retried.

items.stem: Scenario: A request arrives naming a task that the gateway's route table does not list. What does the gateway do?

options.a: Refuses the request, since every task must be registered first
options.b: Uses the most capable model, since the task is unknown
options.c: Holds it until a person adds the task to the policy
options.d: Uses the default entry, since unknown work lands there

items.explanation: The gateway uses the route for the task, and the default for a task the table does not know.

items.stem: Scenario: Users ask about 'E-7310' and the assistant returns a general page about codes, though a page for that very code exists. Which part is likely missing?

options.a: A keyword index, since an identifier is matched by its exact string
options.b: A larger embedding model, since vectors capture exact strings better
options.c: A smaller chunk size, since short chunks match codes more closely
options.d: A reranker alone, since it can find a page that was never retrieved

items.explanation: An embedding index can miss crucial exact matches, so a question that names an identifier needs a keyword index, or both merged by rank.

items.stem: Scenario: A team's files have headings that never name the subject of each section. How can each chunk get the missing context at a low cost?

options.a: Lengthen every chunk until it contains the whole of its document text
options.b: Prepend the file name to every query instead of to the chunks
options.c: A model writes a short orienting sentence per piece, with the source cached
options.d: Drop the chunks that have no context from the index altogether

items.explanation: For text whose structure does not name its subject, a model writes a sentence of about 50-100 tokens per chunk, and prompt caching keeps the one-time cost low.

items.stem: Scenario: On a labelled test, a reply is correct although the evidence passage never came back from the index. How should the team classify it?

options.a: As ok, since a right answer is the goal of the whole system
options.b: As a generation failure, since the model wrote the final answer
options.c: As noise, to be dropped from the denominator of the recall
options.d: As unsupported, a fault in retrieval, since it rests on luck

items.explanation: A right answer without retrieved evidence is a defect in retrieval, because it will not stay right, and it is counted as unsupported.

items.stem: Scenario: A request reaches a company gateway with no sign of who sent it, and it also names a model that is off the list. What verdict does it get?

options.a: Model not allowed, since the list of models is the first rule applied
options.b: Rate limited, since the count of requests is the first rule applied
options.c: Unauthenticated, since the identity check comes ahead of every other rule
options.d: Unknown team, since it is sent to a default set of rules instead

items.explanation: A request with no credential is refused as unauthenticated even when it also asks for a model it may not have, because who is calling comes first.

items.stem: Scenario: A support agent holds a refund tool that no ticket has used in a year. Apart from the tokens its definition takes, what does it add?

options.a: A risk, since every capability is authority that nobody exercises
options.b: A selection benefit, since unused definitions teach the model what to avoid
options.c: A latency benefit, since a longer list lets the model reply faster
options.d: Nothing, since unused definitions are skipped before the request is made

items.explanation: Capability bloat costs context, selection accuracy and risk: each tool is authority, and an unused one is an attack surface.

items.stem: Scenario: An architect compares a custom tool with an MCP server for an internal capability. Which situation favours the server?

options.a: A single application needs it, and the model decides when to call it
options.b: Many different applications must reuse one definition kept by a single team
options.c: The same three steps run in a fixed order in a nightly script
options.d: The counterpart is an independent agent with its own goals and owner

items.explanation: An MCP server gives one definition for many applications. A custom tool serves one application, a direct call a known path, and agent-to-agent an independent agent.

items.stem: Scenario: A platform keeps every trace of errors and slow requests and also a hash-selected 5 percent of the rest. Why keep the 5 percent?

options.a: To lower the chance that any failing trace is missed by chance
options.b: To show what normal looks like, which a store of failures alone cannot
options.c: To meet a rule that retention must be at least five percent
options.d: To make the error and slow traces cheaper to store

items.explanation: The sampled share is what lets you see what normal looks like, which a failure-only store cannot.

items.stem: Scenario: Support at a company asks developers for the identifier that Anthropic's API attaches to each response, so that a failed call can be traced on the provider side. Which is it?

options.a: The traceparent header of the W3C standard, which the API returns to the caller
options.b: The x-api-key header, which names the caller's account
options.c: The request-id header, repeated as a request_id field in error bodies
options.d: The retry-after header, which numbers each attempt

items.explanation: Every API response carries a unique request-id header, and the same identifier is the request_id field in error bodies. The traceparent header ties spans together.

items.stem: Scenario: The number of chunks returned per query falls sharply after a document refresh, while the error rate stays flat. Which layer should the team inspect?

options.a: Retrieval, since the index no longer matches the files
options.b: The model layer, since fewer chunks mean the model reads less
options.c: The tool layer, since tool errors always follow a refresh
options.d: The end-to-end layer, since users must have flagged the change

items.explanation: Retrieval metrics are the chunks returned per query, the share of queries with no hits and the share of chunks older than their source. An error rate does not see them.

items.stem: Scenario: A team measures the share of refund answers that match the policy on a fixed set, with a target of 95 percent. Why is this a good criterion?

options.a: It averages over every type of case, so no case can hide
options.b: It is subjective, so reviewers will accept it
options.c: It has no number, so it can adapt to the traffic
options.d: It is specific, so a release can fail it

items.explanation: A criterion must be one you can fail: specific and measurable, such as 95 percent of refund answers matching the policy on a fixed set.

items.stem: Scenario: A team's evaluation covers accuracy, latency and cost, and the lead asks how it should measure safety and security.

options.a: With the average accuracy over the ordinary cases, since safe answers are accurate ones
options.b: With the mean latency over all cases, since slow answers are safe ones
options.c: With cases built to provoke harmful replies and injection attempts
options.d: With a count of refusals in production, and no test cases written

items.explanation: Safety is the share of harmful or out-of-policy replies on cases built to provoke them, and security the share of injection or leak attempts that got through.

items.stem: Scenario: A team caps the output length and trims the context on day one, before the assistant answers reliably. What does the documentation advise?

options.a: Get a working prompt first, then reduce the delay afterwards
options.b: Cap the length at the start, since early limits show where the quality ends
options.c: Choose the smallest model first, since speed is the main aim
options.d: Skip the quality work, since latency is what users notice

items.explanation: Engineer a prompt that works well first, then try latency reduction; reducing latency prematurely might prevent you from discovering what top performance looks like.

items.stem: Scenario: Cost per answer rose by a third after a migration, and the finance lead suggests shortening every prompt until the old budget fits. What does the page say?

options.a: Shorten the prompts, since quality should not depend on how long they are
options.b: Treat the rise as a billing error and ask the vendor to refund it
options.c: Stay on the old model, since a fixed budget cannot be changed
options.d: Recount tokens and set a new baseline, since price and counts changed

items.explanation: The migration guide says the price per token is higher and the same text produces more tokens: recount tokens and re-baseline cost.

items.stem: Scenario: A gate's latency check uses the nearest-rank 95th percentile of the new timings, and one very slow timing sits in a set of forty. What happens?

options.a: It fails, since the check judges the slowest single timing in the whole set
options.b: It passes if the others meet the limit, as one outlier barely moves the tail
options.c: It fails, since any timing above the limit blocks the change at once
options.d: It passes only if the slow one is removed from the set before the check

items.explanation: The check uses the tail and not the worst case: a single slow case among forty does not block the change, and three do.

items.stem: Scenario: A sponsor suggests waiting for the final date in the retirement notice before deciding on a migration, because the budget is tight. What is the architect's reply?

options.a: Agree, since a lower spend is reason enough to stay on the old model
options.b: Delay hands the choice to the calendar and gives up the way back
options.c: Agree, since the final date is the earliest point at which a plan can be fixed
options.d: Refuse, since the sponsor has no part in migration decisions

items.explanation: Waiting for the retirement date hands the decision to the calendar and gives up the rollback, so the architect states what improves, what it costs and the date.

items.stem: Scenario: A design review asks where a report comparing outcomes across customer groups sits among the four layers of control.

options.a: The input layer, which screens requests before the model sees them
options.b: The output layer, which checks each answer against its source
options.c: The action layer, which approves what the system does in the world
options.d: The monitor layer, which watches results once they exist

items.explanation: A parity report belongs to the monitor layer, which watches drift, groups and alerts after the answers have been produced.

items.stem: Scenario: A team's grounding check is an output control of the ordinary tier and it times out. The answer is a low-consequence reply. What does the course's rule allow?

options.a: To go on, marked so that the gap shows in the record
options.b: To hold the reply until the control is working again
options.c: To go on silently, since the reply is low in consequence
options.d: To send the reply to a person for every future request

items.explanation: Only an output or monitor control of the ordinary tier may proceed with a flag, so that the gap shows in the record; input and action controls hold.

items.stem: Scenario: Beyond being told that AI helped, what should a reader be able to see about an answer?

options.a: The model's full reasoning, with every intermediate step
options.b: The system prompt that was in force, with its hidden rules
options.c: The supporting passage and its version, with a route to a person
options.d: The other customers' answers to the same question

items.explanation: Transparency means telling people and showing the basis: the quote the grounding check used, the document version and the way to reach a person.

items.stem: Scenario: A sponsor's summary runs to 140 words and ends with a list of findings. What should the architect change?

options.a: Keep the length and add a table of the segments below the findings
options.b: Replace it with the engineer's key=value line of figures and costs
options.c: Split it into one separate summary for each stakeholder group
options.d: Shorten it to a plain note of eighty at most, with the single decision

items.explanation: The sponsor stops reading early, so the summary is plain, at most 80 words, and ends with the one decision asked.

items.stem: Scenario: The recommended option in a record is the newest and most capable design, though a cheaper one meets every service level. What is the fault?

options.a: The recommended design should be the one with the fastest answers
options.b: The record should recommend two options so that the sponsor can choose
options.c: The pick must be the lowest-priced candidate that clears every target
options.d: The newest design should be recommended whenever it is affordable

items.explanation: The recommended option is the cheapest one that meets the service levels; capability beyond the requirement is cost without a requirement behind it.

items.stem: Scenario: A pilot table's test counts escalations to a person for each hundred disputes. Which assumption does it check?

options.a: That staff patched edge cases manually, which will not scale
options.b: That the inputs in the trial were typical of production traffic
options.c: That the capacity of the platform was never close to its limits
options.d: That reviewers could keep up with the volume of items

items.explanation: Each assumption of a pilot has its own test and stop trigger; counting escalations per 100 disputes tests whether staff covered the edge cases by hand.

items.stem: Scenario: A company needs a restriction that reaches every developer and that no developer's own file can override. Where does it belong?

options.a: In the shared project file that every developer receives
options.b: In managed settings, which rank above every other level
options.c: In each developer's user file, set during onboarding
options.d: In the project local file, which is read last

items.explanation: Managed settings apply above every other level, so no user, project or local value overrides them, with a few security exceptions.

items.stem: Scenario: A user file and a project file each list some permission rules, and no lock is set. What is the effective list?

options.a: Only the project file's list, since the shared file is closest to the work
options.b: The two combined, with duplicates dropped
options.c: Only the user file's list, since the user level was set later
options.d: Neither, since conflicting lists cancel each other out

items.explanation: List settings combine across files without duplicates; only a lock such as allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly stops the merge.

items.stem: Scenario: A company has no device management for its laptops but wants to deliver one Claude Code policy. What does the documentation offer?

options.a: A file in each repository that developers are not able to edit
options.b: A per-group policy that is chosen in the console for each team
options.c: Settings fetched from the console at launch and refreshed hourly
options.d: A setting kept inside each developer's own user file or profile

items.explanation: Server-managed settings are fetched at startup and polled hourly for Teams and Enterprise; per-group policy is not yet supported.

items.stem: Scenario: A security lead asks what an empty strictKnownMarketplaces value means for plugins.

options.a: It shuts out all sources, the official one included
options.b: It allows every source, since nothing is listed to restrict
options.c: It allows only the official source, since that is the default
options.d: It is invalid, and Claude Code falls back to the user's own list

items.explanation: An empty list blocks every source, the official marketplace included, so allow nothing and allow ours are different lists.

items.stem: Scenario: A platform team will measure the effect of a Claude Code rollout on time to merge. What should it record before the first developer starts?

options.a: A single week of data, taken the week before the rollout
options.b: No baseline, since the dashboard will show the change by itself
options.c: The count of lines accepted, which gives a baseline for activity
options.d: Four weeks of baseline data, enough to span a release cycle

items.explanation: A target on an outcome needs a baseline, and four weeks of data include a release cycle and a quiet week.

items.stem: Scenario: A team wants the share of its merged pull requests that Claude Code helped to write. Which source gives it?

options.a: The lines-accepted usage metric, which counts suggestions in sessions
options.b: The spend report CSV, which lists the cost for each member
options.c: Contribution metrics on the analytics dashboard, via the GitHub app
options.d: The daily active users chart, which counts sessions

items.explanation: Contribution metrics, such as merged pull requests with Claude Code assistance, need the GitHub app and are not available with zero data retention.

items.stem: Scenario: In the capstone's chain, a passage has come back once barred material was removed. Which step follows?

options.a: A test that it was taken from the current edition of its source
options.b: The routing of the answer to a person or to automatic sending
options.c: The tokenising of identifiers found in the question text
options.d: The release gate that judges the protected segment

items.explanation: The chain runs tokenise, retrieve by rights, check the version, check the source, route, then trace; each step answers one failure.

items.stem: Scenario: A review produced findings: one in P3, two in P5 and none elsewhere. What is its scorecard?

options.a: 1, 2 in the order of the findings, with no zero entries
options.b: 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0, since the larger count goes first
options.c: 3, the total number of findings
options.d: 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 0 for the domains P1 to P7

items.explanation: The scorecard is a count of findings per domain in the order P1 to P7, with a zero for a domain that has no finding.

items.stem: Scenario: The review computes the accuracy a design needs for an error cost of 5 and a review cost of 6. What does it return?

options.a: -20, the figure that the formula gives before any clamp
options.b: 0, since a check dearer than the mistake never pays
options.c: 100, since the check is dearer than the error
options.d: 17, the difference of the two costs in percent

items.explanation: The needed accuracy is never below 0: a check that costs as much as an error, or more, needs no accuracy.
